cls: Anti-CGRP receptor monoclonal antibody - migraine preventive
pharm: Human IgG2 monoclonal antibody that binds and antagonizes the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor, reducing CGRP-mediated signaling implicated in migraine.
quick: 70 mg subcutaneously once monthly; some patients benefit from 140 mg once monthly
Subcutaneous injection; not related to meals
No adequate human data; long half-life - discuss risks/benefits
No data on milk transfer; IgG antibodies are minimally absorbed orally by infants
No dose adjustment expected (monoclonal antibody, not renally cleared)
No dose adjustment expected (catabolized like other antibodies)
Hypersensitivity reactions, constipation (including serious), new/worsening hypertension
summary: Erenumab is a human monoclonal antibody that blocks the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor, indicated for the preventive treatment of migraine in adults. It is given as a subcutaneous injection of 70 mg once monthly, with 140 mg once monthly used in some patients. By antagonizing the CGRP receptor it reduces the vasodilatory and pain-signaling effects of CGRP that are central to migraine attacks. It is generally well tolerated; the most common adverse reactions are injection-site reactions and constipation. Important warnings include hypersensitivity reactions (which may occur hours to more than a week after a dose), serious constipation (occasionally requiring hospitalization or surgery), and new-onset or worsening hypertension reported post-marketing; development or worsening of Raynaud phenomenon has also been reported. It is not metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes, so small-molecule drug interactions are minimal.
indications: Preventive treatment of migraine in adults

dosage.d: 140 mg subcutaneously once monthly (given as two consecutive 70 mg injections)
dosage.n: Some patients may benefit from 140 mg

admin: Administer by subcutaneous injection in the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm (do not inject into areas where the skin is tender, bruised, red or hard)
For the 140 mg dose, give two separate 70 mg injections consecutively
Remove from the refrigerator and allow to sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes before injecting; do not warm by other means and do not shake
Inspect the solution; do not use if cloudy, discolored or contains particles
Patients may self-administer after proper training in subcutaneous technique
moa: Erenumab is a human IgG2 monoclonal antibody that binds to the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor and competitively antagonizes its function. CGRP is a neuropeptide that is released during migraine attacks and produces vasodilation and transmission of nociceptive (pain) signals within the trigeminovascular system. By blocking the CGRP receptor, erenumab inhibits CGRP-mediated signaling, reducing the frequency of migraine attacks. As a monoclonal antibody it is not metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes and is eliminated through proteolytic catabolism.

absolute: Serious hypersensitivity to erenumab or any excipient (e.g., anaphylaxis, angioedema)
relative: History of severe constipation or conditions predisposing to bowel obstruction
Raynaud phenomenon or significant peripheral vascular disease
Latex sensitivity (the needle cap of some prefilled devices contains dry natural rubber)
monitor: Hypersensitivity reactions (may occur hours to >1 week after dosing)
Blood pressure for new-onset or worsening hypertension

preg: There are no adequate data on erenumab use in pregnant women to inform a drug-associated risk; animal studies showed no adverse developmental effects at exposures well above human levels. Given its long half-life, consider the prolonged exposure when planning pregnancy; a pregnancy exposure registry is available.
lact: There are no data on the presence of erenumab in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or on milk production. Human IgG is present in milk but is largely degraded in the infant gastrointestinal tract and minimally absorbed; weigh developmental/health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and any risk.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed. Erenumab is a monoclonal antibody not eliminated by the kidneys; severe renal impairment was not specifically studied but is not expected to affect exposure.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is needed. As an antibody, erenumab is cleared by proteolytic catabolism rather than hepatic metabolism; hepatic impairment is not expected to alter its pharmacokinetics.

major: No clinically significant major drug interactions identified
moderate: No clinically significant moderate interactions established (not a CYP450 substrate/inhibitor/inducer)
minor: No effect on the pharmacokinetics of oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol/norgestimate) or sumatriptan
interactions.diagnostics: No specific laboratory interference identified; monitor blood pressure clinically.

serious: Serious constipation with complications (including some requiring hospitalization or surgery, rare bowel obstruction)
Hypersensitivity reactions including rash, angioedema and anaphylaxis

monitoring: Watch for hypersensitivity reactions, which may occur hours to more than a week after administration
Monitor bowel function; advise about constipation and seek care for severe or persistent constipation
Monitor blood pressure for new-onset or worsening hypertension
Assess for symptoms of Raynaud phenomenon (cold, color change, pain in fingers/toes)
Assess migraine frequency response after several months to judge continued benefit
counsel: This medicine is used to prevent migraines, not to treat an attack that has already started; continue any rescue medicines as directed
Inject once a month under the skin of the abdomen, thigh or upper arm; let the pen/syringe warm at room temperature for at least 30 minutes first and do not shake it
Constipation is common - increase fluids and fiber; tell your doctor about severe or persistent constipation or abdominal pain
Seek immediate care for swelling of the face/lips/tongue, trouble breathing, or rash (allergic reaction); report color changes or pain in fingers/toes
Tell your doctor if you have high blood pressure or develop new high blood pressure, and if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding
pk: Reduction in migraine frequency typically begins within the first month of dosing
Peak serum concentration at approximately 6 days after subcutaneous injection
Refrigerate at 2-8 C (36-46 F) in original carton; may be kept at room temperature up to 25 C for up to 7 days; do not freeze or shake; protect from light
pearls: Anti-CGRP RECEPTOR monoclonal antibody for migraine PROPHYLAXIS (not acute attack treatment); once-monthly subcutaneous dosing
Watch for serious constipation - rare cases required hospitalization or surgery; counsel patients proactively
Hypersensitivity reactions can be delayed (hours to more than a week after a dose)
New-onset or worsening hypertension and Raynaud phenomenon reported post-marketing
Long ~28-day half-life; minimal drug interactions (not CYP450 metabolized) - no effect on oral contraceptives or sumatriptan
missed: If a dose is missed, administer it as soon as possible. After that, schedule the next monthly dose from the date of the late dose (i.e., reset the monthly schedule from the day the missed dose was given); do not give two doses to make up for a missed one.
overdose: There is no specific information on overdose with erenumab and no specific antidote. Doses up to 280 mg have been administered subcutaneously in studies without dose-limiting toxicity. In the event of overdose, monitor the patient for any signs or symptoms of adverse reactions and provide appropriate symptomatic and supportive care.
